title: Volkswagen Mission Efficiency Concept Is a Near-Production EV Follow-up to the XL1

body_markdown:
In 2013, Volkswagen launched a limited-production model called XL1 that was celebrated as the world’s most efficient street-legal car. Fast-forward to 2026, and the Volkswagen Mission Efficiency concept takes the next step in development by exploring the upper limits of EV efficiency. It uses numerous off-the-shelf parts, and it’s headed to production.


The wing-shaped profile with covered rear wheels and a tapered rear end reminds us of the XL1, and the front end is XL1-like as well. That’s likely not a coincidence: Volkswagen wanted to make the Mission Efficiency as aerodynamic as possible, and there are limited ways to achieve that goal. The coupe posts a drag coefficient of 0.158 compared to 0.159 for the XL1. For context, the 2022[Mercedes-Benz Vision EQXX](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/the-manifold/2022-01-04/) concept that was also designed with maximum efficiency in mind had a 0.17 drag coefficient.


Volkswagen claims that the 0.158 drag coefficient is a record for a road-approved car. That’s the first of three records set by the Mission Efficiency. It also returned an electricity consumption of 6.48 kWh per 100 km (that’s 62 miles) during what the brand calls the “ideal trip,” meaning the car was driving at a constant 42 mph, on a route without hills, and without air conditioning or other features that drain energy. The third record is that the design study is the most economical near-production EV in its class.


The ideal trip seldom happens, however, and real-world numbers are far more telling. Volkswagen drove the prototype from its hometown of Wolfsburg, Germany, to Vienna, Austria, via Poland and the Czech Republic. The average speed during the 794-mile trip was about 42 mph, and the top speed achieved was around 86 mph. The Mission Efficiency stopped to charge once, and it arrived in the Austrian capital with about 101 miles of range left.

Volkswagen added a 370-watt solar system to the roof and the trunk lid to run power-draining features like the air conditioning and the heater. This system can also add up to 18 miles of range a day if it’s sunny enough outside (sorry, Seattleites).


Based on the MEB+ platform, the Mission Efficiency shares its electric drivetrain with[the ID. Polo](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/volkswagen-id-polo-interior-buttons/) , which is a small hatchback sold in Europe. The system consists of a front-mounted electric motor that draws electricity from a 54.9-kilowatt-hour lithium-ion battery pack to zap the front wheels with about 135 horsepower. The front axle and the front hydraulic braking system come from the Polo as well, but the rear axle features a new, innovative electromechanical braking system without brake lines to save weight.


The interior was developed to be as light as possible as well. It features lightweight panels, a removable Bluetooth-compatible speaker instead of a conventional sound system, and a dock for a smartphone or a tablet that replaces the touchscreen on the center console. There are four seats, though the rear seats are only suitable for small children, and about 17 cubic feet of trunk space. Those figures are a little surprising when you consider that this is not exactly a small car: At about 188 inches long and 55 inches tall, it’s about as big as[the outgoing BMW 3 Series](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/2019-bmw-3-series-first-drive/) (185 inches and 57 inches tall). The concept’s weight hasn’t been released.


There’s no word yet on what the future holds for the Volkswagen Mission Efficiency concept, but the brand stresses that it’s a near-production car, so we’re guessing that it has already received the proverbial green light for production. Pricing and availability will be announced later. For context, the diesel-electric XL1 cost a little over €110,000 in Germany, and was limited to 250 units.


In an alternate universe, the follow-up to the XL1 could have looked and sounded a lot different than the Mission Efficiency. In 2014, Volkswagen traveled to the Paris auto show to introduce[an XL1-based concept called XL Sport](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/petersen-automotive-museum-vw-electric-future/) that used a 1.2-liter four-cylinder engine borrowed from the Ducati 1199 Superleggera and rated at 200 horsepower. Quick, low, and light thanks to carbon fiber, the coupe was considered for limited production but ultimately canned as Volkswagen cut costs in the wake of Dieselgate.
